name: Sabaic
confidence_why: Sabaic survives only in a consonantal script with no oral tradition, and Nebes and Stein (2008) state outright that no conclusions are possible about its accent, which Kogan and Korotayev (1997) independently confirm, so the record correctly leaves the stress system undetermined.
catalog_citation: Nebes, Norbert & Peter Stein. 2008. Ancient South Arabian. In Roger D. Woodard (ed.), The Ancient Languages of Syria-Palestine and Arabia, 145-178. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
catalog_quote: 3.1 Preliminary remarks. The Ancient South Arabian writing system is, like that of many other Semitic languages, primarily devised for the representation of consonants, and expresses vowels only in very restricted cases. In the absence of an oral tradition, the precise pronunciation of its graphemes is unknown, and a conventional reconstruction of the sound values is possible only by comparison with other Semitic languages. ... 3.3 Vowels. The few statements that can be made about the vocalization of Ancient South Arabian are based on the use of the glides w and y. ... Apart from these few hints, practically nothing is known about the vocalization of the Ancient South Arabian texts preserved for us. The question of a possible differentiation of syllables according to vowel quantity, therefore, likewise cannot be answered with certainty, nor are any broad conclusions possible concerning the accentual relationships of Ancient South Arabian.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule: the language is attested only in a consonantal script with no oral tradition, so vowel quantity, syllable structure and accent cannot be recovered; the authoritative modern sketch states explicitly that no conclusions about accent are possible.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Kogan & Korotayev 1997: 224 speculate only that the Minaic 'parasitic' h reflects 'a peculiar character of the stress (possibly even pitch)', without locating stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Applies to Ancient South Arabian as a whole (Sabaic, Minaic, Qatabanic, Hadramitic), with Sabaic the base of the description; epigraphic texts only, no citation forms exist.
new_statements.identity_note: Sabaic is an extinct epigraphic language (c. 8th c. BCE - 6th c. CE) known only from a purely consonantal script. The deciding source describes Ancient South Arabian as a whole with Sabaic as its base; the Kogan & Korotayev 1997 remark on stress concerns Minaic (mina1268 family area; Glottolog Minaic) rather than Sabaic specifically. Sister Glottolog codes held under source_audit: mina1267/1268/1269, hadr1235/1236, saba1265/1267/1268/1276.
